title: Kaaba
def: The cube-shaped House in the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, built by Abraham and Ishmael, toward which Muslims face in prayer.
what: “The first House established for people was that at Bakka, blessed and a guidance to the worlds” (3:96). Abraham and Ishmael raised its foundations (2:127), and God made it “a place of return for people and a sanctuary” (2:125). It stands empty, with a black cloth cover renewed each year, and is circled seven times in tawaf. Muslims worldwide pray toward it (2:144), which unites them in direction while they worship God alone and not the house.
misread: Muslims do not worship the Kaaba or the Black Stone. Umar is reported to have said at the Stone: “I know you are only a stone that cannot harm or benefit; had I not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not” (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Kafir
def: One who rejects or denies the truth; literally, one who covers it up.
what: The root k-f-r means “to cover”. The Quran uses a related word for farmers, who cover seed with soil (57:20). As a religious term it describes a person who knows the truth and hides or rejects it, and it is a statement about belief, not a name for a people.

Chapter 109 ends “to you your religion, and to me mine”. The Quran does not forbid kindness and justice to those who do not fight Muslims over religion, and it says God loves those who act justly (60:8).
misread: That it is a slur, or a licence to kill anyone who is not a Muslim.
sources: The decision about who has rejected God is left to God. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari warns that if a man calls his brother “kafir”, one of them has earned the word, and jurists accordingly forbade accusing Muslims of disbelief lightly. The Quran also gives separate words for the People of the Book and for polytheists, and does not use one label for all.

title: Kafur
def: A fragrant, cooling spring in Paradise, named in the Quran (76:5).
what: “The righteous will drink from a cup mixed with kafur, a spring from which God’s servants drink, making it flow in abundance” (76:5–6). The word means camphor in Arabic; the Quran uses it as an image of coolness and fragrance in Paradise.

title: Khadija
def: The first wife of the Prophet and the first person to accept Islam.
what: Khadija bint Khuwaylid was a respected businesswoman of Mecca who employed Muhammad as her agent, and later proposed marriage to him. When he came back trembling from the cave of Hira, she consoled him: “You keep ties of kin, bear the burdens of the weak, help the poor and support those struck by calamity” (Sahih al-Bukhari). She believed first, spent her wealth for the cause, and died in 619, the “year of sorrow”. Gabriel sent her greetings from her Lord, according to Sahih al-Bukhari.
sources: The Prophet married no other woman while she lived. Aisha said she was never as jealous of anyone as of Khadija, from the Prophet’s frequent praise of her (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Khalifites
def: A small modern movement following Rashad Khalifa (d. 1990) that accepts only the Quran, and which Muslim scholars regard as outside the mainstream.
what: Rashad Khalifa, an Egyptian-American biochemist, claimed to have found a numerical code based on 19 in the Quran, and rejected the hadith. He denied the last two verses of Surah 9. Muslim scholars across the schools reject these claims, since the Quran itself tells believers to obey the Messenger (4:59, 59:7), and the verses were recited and written down from the time of the Prophet.

title: Kharijites
def: An early group who seceded from Ali’s army after Siffin (657), and who held that a Muslim committing a major sin ceases to be a believer.
what: After Ali agreed to arbitration with Muawiya they left, saying “judgement belongs only to God”, and turned against both. They killed Ali in 661. The Prophet foretold a people who would recite the Quran without it passing their throats, and would leave religion like an arrow from its game (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim), and the mainstream understood this to mean them.
sources: Mainstream scholars made the Kharijite excess an object lesson: declaring other Muslims unbelievers (takfir) for sin is the error the Kharijites made and that the main schools have always warned against. The Ibadi school of Oman, which descends from moderate early Kharijism, rejects the extremist label.

title: Khawf
def: Fear of God in Islam is joined with hope and love, and the Prophet taught that God’s mercy outstrips His wrath.
what: The Quran says “fear Me, if you are believers” (3:175), and also “do not despair of the mercy of God” (39:53). The Prophet said that God wrote, before creating the world, “My mercy outstrips My wrath” (Sahih al-Bukhari). Scholars say a believer should be like a bird with two wings, fear and hope.

title: Khaybar
def: An oasis north of Medina, where Muslims fought a campaign in 628–629 against a fortified group of the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir and others.
what: After the Treaty of Hudaybiyya the Prophet marched against Khaybar, whose people had joined the coalition against Medina at the Trench. The fortresses fell after weeks of siege, and he let the inhabitants stay and work the date palms for half the produce. The Quran refers to the victory in 48:18–21.
sources: Reports differ about the terms and the later events, including the poisoned lamb offered to the Prophet and the order of Umar in 641 to remove the Jews of Khaybar from Arabia. Historians read them in the context of the war, and the hostilities arose from the alliance with the enemies of Medina.

title: Khidr
def: A servant of God, named in the Quran only as one of “Our servants” (18:65), whose journey with Moses is told in chapter 18.
what: Moses met “a servant of Ours to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught knowledge from Us” (18:65), and asked to follow him to learn. The man damaged a boat, killed a boy and rebuilt a wall, each for a reason he explained afterwards. Moses could not be patient, and so they parted (18:60–82). The Prophet named him Khidr in a hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: Scholars differ on whether Khidr was a prophet, a saint or an angel, and whether he is alive. The story’s point is that a human being’s knowledge is limited, and that what looks like harm may hold a hidden good.

title: Killing
def: The Quran forbids killing and says that taking one life unjustly is as if one had killed all of humanity.
what: “Whoever kills a person, other than for murder or corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all people; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all people” (5:32). “Do not kill the soul that God has made sacred except by right” (17:33; 6:151; 25:68). The law of equal retribution (2:178) includes the encouragement to forgive (2:178, 42:40) and blood-money. Women, children and the elderly may not be killed in war (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: Classical jurists required a court and due proof for a death sentence; the Prophet said that the first matters judged on the Day of Judgement will be blood-shed (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Kindness
def: Kindness to parents, kin, neighbours, orphans and the poor, a duty throughout the Quran.
what: “Worship God and associate nothing with Him; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the neighbour near and far, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those your right hands possess” (4:36). The Prophet said: “He who is not merciful to others will not be shown mercy” (Sahih al-Bukhari), and “God is kind and loves kindness in all things” (Sahih Muslim). The Prophet was sent “as a mercy to the worlds” (21:107).

title: Kitab
def: The word for “book” in Arabic, used for the Quran, for earlier scripture and for God’s record of all things.
what: The Quran is “the Book, in which is no doubt” (2:2). It speaks of God sending scripture to earlier prophets, such as the Torah to Moses and the Gospel to Jesus (3:3–4), and of the “Mother of the Book” (43:4), the source. Believers have faith in the books of God (2:285). The record of deeds is also a kitab (18:49).
sources: Some scholars of Arabic think the word came from Aramaic or Akkadian roots; Muslims scholars note that Arabic has borrowed words, as other languages do, and that this does not alter its meaning.

title: Knowledge
def: Seeking knowledge is a duty in Islam, from the first word of revelation, “Read”.
what: The first revelation was “Read in the name of your Lord who created… who taught by the pen” (96:1–5). “Say: are those who know equal to those who do not know?” (39:9). The Prophet said that seeking knowledge is a duty on every Muslim (Ibn Majah), and that the path to knowledge is a path to Paradise (Sahih Muslim). The Quran asks people to study creation (3:190–191) and to travel to see (29:20).

title: Kubrawiyya
def: A Sufi order founded by Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 1221) in Central Asia, which is also found among Muslims in China.
what: Najm al-Din Kubra of Khwarazm taught a method of remembrance with visions of colours and the stages of the soul, and died fighting the Mongols at the fall of Khiva. His order spread to Persia, India and China, where Dru Gladney found it small among the Hui.

title: Kufr
def: Disbelief, or ingratitude: literally “covering” the truth, in the heart or in deed.
what: “Kafara” means to cover, as a farmer covers seed, and the Quran uses it of rejecting the truth and also of being ungrateful for God’s favours (14:7, 27:40). Kufr in this sense can be of belief or of behaviour. It is not for people to decide in whose heart faith lies: the Prophet warned that whoever calls his brother a disbeliever, it returns on one of them (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Kutub
def: The scriptures God revealed: the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Quran.
what: Belief in the scriptures is one of the six articles of faith, in the hadith of Gabriel (Sahih Muslim). The Quran names the Torah given to Moses (5:44), the Psalms (Zabūr) given to David (4:163), the Gospel given to Jesus, and the scrolls of Abraham and Moses (87:18–19). “We make no distinction between any of His messengers” (2:285).
misread: That Islam is a rival religion that sets out to cancel Judaism and Christianity.
sources: The Quran presents itself as confirming what came before it and guarding it (5:48), and as the same message from the same God. Muslims do not hold that the earlier prophets taught something else. Their claim is that the message was one, was corrupted or misunderstood in places, and was finally given in a form kept intact.

title: Kabbara
def: To proclaim, in the prayer or otherwise, that God is the Greater: to say Allāhu akbar.
what: Kabbara means to declare God’s greatness by saying Allāhu akbar, “God is the Greater”. The noun is takbīr. The Quran commands: “Your Lord, magnify Him” (74:3), and “Magnify Him with a great magnification” (17:111). Faruqi defines the verb as proclaiming, within worship or outside it, that God is the Greater. The takbīr opens the ritual prayer, marks movements within it, and is called in the adhān. Muslims also say it at the festival prayers of ʿĪd, during the days of the pilgrimage, and in daily life when they see something wonderful or meet a difficulty. It reminds the speaker that God is greater than every worldly thing.
misread: It is often presented in the media as a battle cry, whereas Muslims say it in prayer, at festivals and in everyday life.

title: Kafara
def: To deny in declared words that God is God, that Muhammad is His Prophet, or that the Quran is wholly God’s truth and revelation.
what: The root k-f-r means to cover or to deny. In religious use kafara means to reject faith openly. Faruqi gives the sense of solemnly saying that God is not God, or that He lacks any of His attributes, that Muhammad (peace be upon him) is not the Prophet of God, or that anything in the Quran is not verbatim truth and revelation from God. The noun is kufr and the one who does it is a kāfir. Jurists urge great care in applying it. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim warns that if a man calls his brother a kāfir, the charge falls on one of them.
misread: It is rendered “infidel” in older English, a word that carries a sense of contempt that the Arabic term does not have.

title: Khabir, al-
def: A divine name: the All-Aware, who knows the inner reality of all things.
what: Al-Khabīr is one of the names of God. It means the One who is fully aware, whose knowledge reaches the inner nature of things. The Quran pairs it often with other names: “He is the Wise, the All-Aware” (6:18; 34:1), and it says of Him, “Does He who created not know? He is the Subtle, the All-Aware” (67:14). The name tells believers that nothing escapes God, neither deeds, nor intentions, nor what lies hidden in hearts. Scholars teach that it brings reassurance to those wronged and a warning to those who do wrong in secret. Faruqi glosses it as the All-Knowing, and it is close in sense to al-ʿAlīm, with the stress on awareness of inner detail.

title: Khabith, al-
def: What is foul and evil: whatever goes against God’s will and is judged bad and wrong.
what: Al-khabīth is that which is bad, foul or evil. Faruqi defines it as what goes against the will of God and is counted as bad, wrong and evil. The Quran sets it against al-ṭayyib, the good and pure: “Say: the bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the bad pleases you” (5:100). The Prophet (peace be upon him) is described as one who “makes lawful for them the good things and forbids for them the foul” (7:157). The word covers wrong things in food, conduct and character, and jurists use it when they discuss what is forbidden. Its plural, khabāʾith, means wicked deeds.

title: Khabithah, al-
def: The feminine form of khabīth, meaning a deed, word or thing that is foul, impure or bad; its plural is khabāʾith.
what: Khabīth means foul, impure or bad, and it is the opposite of ṭayyib, which means wholesome and pure. Al-khabīthah is the feminine form with the article, and it names a deed, word or thing that has this quality; its plural is khabāʾith. The Quran uses the root in several settings. It likens an evil word to an evil tree (14:26), it calls the shameful acts of the people of Lot khabāʾith (21:74), and it says that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) makes good things lawful and foul things unlawful (7:157). The word therefore joins moral badness and physical impurity in one term.
misread: Rendering it only as “evil” hides that the word also covers what is physically foul or impure, not just what is morally bad.

title: Khalifah
def: The vicegerent of God in space and time; the word is also used for the successor who leads the Muslim community.
what: Khalīfah comes from a root meaning to succeed or to stand in the place of another. The Quran uses it when God tells the angels, “I am placing on the earth a khalīfah” (2:30), and it addresses David with the same word (38:26). In this sense the human being holds the earth as a trust, answerable to God for how it is used. The same word came to mean the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad (peace be upon him), beginning with Abu Bakr, who was called khalīfat rasūl Allāh, the successor of the Messenger of God. English “caliph” is the usual form of this second sense.
misread: Translating it as “successor” or “caliph” alone loses the Quranic sense of the human being as God’s vicegerent on earth.
sources: The classical commentators differ on who is meant in 2:30: some take it to be Adam and his descendants, and some take it to mean a people who succeed one another. All agree that it describes a responsibility given by God and not a share in His authority.

title: Khaliq, al-
def: A divine name meaning the Creator, the One who brings things into being from nothing and gives each its measure.
what: Al-Khāliq, the Creator, is one of the names of God. The Quran uses it in the verse, “He is God, the Creator, the Maker, the Fashioner” (59:24), and says, “God is the Creator of all things” (13:16). The root kh-l-q carries the sense of bringing into existence and of giving a measure or proportion, and the same verb is used for the creation of the heavens and the earth. Muslims use the name to affirm that everything other than God was created and depends on Him. For that reason the Quran presents worship of anything created as a mistake about what is real, and it asks its hearers to look at the creation as a sign of its Creator.
misread: The name is often translated “the Creator” as though it meant a first cause that then withdraws; the Quran presents God as continually sustaining what He created.

title: Khayr
def: The good, meaning whatever is good in the sight of God, including wealth, deeds, and what leads a person to Him.
what: Khayr is the general Arabic word for good and for what is better. The Quran uses it for moral good: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it” (99:7). It also uses it for the best course of action, as in the call to “invite to the good” (3:104), and for the guidance that is sent from God (2:105). In a few places it is used for wealth, as in the verse that speaks of leaving khayr for one’s heirs (2:180).

Muslims use the word in everyday speech too. A person may say jazāk Allāhu khayran, “may God reward you with good”, as thanks, and inshāʾ Allāh khayr, “if God wills, it is for the good”, when the outcome is not yet known. In both cases the speaker treats God as the source of whatever good comes, which matches the Quranic use of the word.
misread: A single English word such as “good” hides that khayr is measured by what God has commanded and approved, and not by custom or personal taste.
sources: The Quran says that a person may dislike a thing in which God has placed much khayr (4:19), and it teaches that good which is done for God is never lost (3:115).

title: Khaza
def: To bring shame and disgrace on a person who breaks the commandments of God, in this world and in the next; the verbal noun is khizy.
what: Khazā means to disgrace or to put to shame, and its verbal noun is khizy, disgrace. The Quran uses it of the humiliation that follows rebellion against God, and it speaks of disgrace in this world and a greater punishment in the next (5:33). It also appears in prayers. Believers ask God not to disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection (3:194), and they say, “Our Lord, whomever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced” (3:192). The word names a public and inward shame, one that falls on the person who has broken God’s commandments and been shown to have done so. It is the opposite of the honour that God gives to those who obey Him.
misread: It is often translated plainly as “humiliation” or “disgrace”, which loses that the Quran ties this shame to breaking God’s commandments and to the Day of Judgement.

title: Khilafah
def: The institution of man as God’s vicegerent on earth, and the government that continued the worldly rule of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
what: Khilāfah is the noun for the office or institution of the khalīfah. It has two senses. The first is the human responsibility, given by God, to act as His vicegerent on earth (2:30). The second is the government that carried on the worldly leadership of Muhammad (peace be upon him) after his death, beginning with Abu Bakr, then Umar, Uthman and Ali. These four are called the rightly guided caliphs. Later dynasties, including the Umayyads, Abbasids and Ottomans, also held the office. The consultation of the community in choosing and advising its leader is linked in the Quran to the principle of shūrā (42:38).
misread: “Caliphate” in English news writing usually means a state of one ruler; the word in Arabic also names the human duty of stewardship over the earth.
sources: Scholars of the classical period, such as al-Mawardi, wrote works on the office, and they differed on how the khalīfah should be chosen. Muslims today hold different views on whether the institution should be revived.

title: Kitab, al-
def: “The Book”, used in the Quran for the Quran itself; the word also names earlier scriptures and the record of what God has decreed.
what: Al-Kitāb means “the Book”, from a root meaning to write. The Quran opens its second surah, “This is the Book, in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing” (2:2), and in this use the word names the Quran itself. Faruqi lists it as another name for al-Qurʾān al-Karīm, the Noble Quran. The word is also used in other ways. The Quran calls the earlier scriptures given to Moses and Jesus kitāb, and it calls their followers ahl al-kitāb, the People of the Book. It also speaks of a record in which God’s decree and each person’s deeds are written.
misread: Reading it only as “book” as in any printed volume hides that the Quran uses the word as a name of the revelation itself.
